c.tagline: A red-ochre Saharan oasis town of mudbrick architecture, palm groves, and a shimmering salt lake

taxi.fareNote: Most sightseeing is arranged as a half or full-day tour rather than metered taxi rides

emergency.note: Dial 17 for police and 14 for medical/fire emergencies; French is more useful than English with dispatchers

walk: The ksar and market area are walkable; the salt lake viewpoint and surrounding dune villages require a car or organized tour

safety.safety: Generally calm and welcoming to visitors, though remote; check current travel advisories for southern Algeria before visiting
safety.crime: Low crime; main risks relate to desert heat and remoteness rather than crime

hood_landmark.Old Ksar (Red Town): Timimoun's red ochre mudbrick old town
hood_landmark.Palm Oasis: The palm grove and traditional foggara irrigation channels

avoid.reason: Do not head into the open desert or toward border zones without authorized guides — surrounding Saharan areas are under security restrictions and often require police-notified itineraries.

hood_desc: The town's iconic red mudbrick old quarter, with distinctive Sudanese-influenced architecture found nowhere else in Algeria.
The palm grove sustaining the town, still watered by an ancient underground foggara canal system.
The commercial center with the covered market and most hotels and restaurants.

water.note: Stick to bottled water in Saharan oasis towns.

transit.sys: Local taxis and guide-arranged vehicles; no formal bus network
transit.pay: Cash to the driver or guide
transit.map: Not centrally published; hotels and tour agencies arrange transport
transit.note: A local guide is recommended for dune excursions and visits to outlying ksour villages

transport.air: Timimoun Airport (TMX), about 5 km from town
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect to Adrar and onward to Algiers
transport.car: The N51 highway connects Timimoun to the regional road network

net.m: Moderate 3G/4G in town, no coverage in the surrounding desert
net.w: Wifi available in some hotels but often slow
net.gb: ~$5-10 for a prepaid tourist SIM (passport required to register)
net.fwn: Wifi available in central hotels, though unreliable
net.ap: A Mobilis or Djezzy prepaid SIM, registered with your passport

tip.s: 10% is customary and appreciated for desert guides
tip.r: Rounding up or 5-10% is appreciated, not obligatory

food.name: Gourara dates
food.desc: The oasis lives on its palms: Deglet Nour, Feggous and Tinnaser dates eaten fresh, dried or crushed into paste, often with buttermilk or dry cheese.

places.name: Timimoun central souk
places.area: Town centre, near the main street
places.note: Date stalls sell several varieties by the kilo; autumn harvest is the best time to buy.

places.name: Palmeraie gardens below the ksar
places.note: Growers working the foggara irrigation channels sell straight from the trees.

places.name: Hotel Gourara
places.note: Red-ochre hotel with palmeraie views; dates and tea come with every meal.

food.name: Saharan couscous
food.desc: Steamed semolina under a stew of lamb or camel with carrot, turnip and chickpeas, sometimes enriched with dried meat; the Friday and feast-day dish.

places.name: Hotel Gourara restaurant
places.note: The town's most reliable dining room, with a set Algerian menu and good bourek.

places.name: Hotel de l'Oasis Rouge
places.note: Historic red-earth hotel a few minutes away; simple Algerian cooking in a landmark building.

places.name: Guesthouses in the ksour
places.note: Family maisons d'hotes in the old villages cook couscous for guests on request.

food.name: Chorba frik
food.desc: Soup of green cracked wheat with lamb, tomato, chickpeas and coriander, thick and warming against the cold desert nights and the daily meal in Ramadan.

places.name: Hotel Gourara restaurant
places.note: Chorba opens most evening menus, followed by bourek and grilled meat.

places.name: Town centre cafes, Rue Principale
places.note: Small cafes near the souk serve chorba with bread for a few dinars.

places.name: Hotel de l'Oasis Rouge
places.note: Straightforward soups and stews in the dining room of Timimoun's old colonial hotel.

food.name: Kesra and ash-baked bread
food.desc: Flat semolina bread cooked on a griddle or buried in hot ash and sand, torn by hand and used to scoop up stew, oil or date paste.

places.name: Timimoun central souk
places.note: Bakers and home cooks sell warm kesra in the mornings beside the vegetable stalls.

places.name: Guesthouses in the ksour
places.note: Village hosts still bake bread in ash; the best chance to see it done.

places.name: Desert camps, erg west of Timimoun
places.note: Overnight dune camps bake bread in the fire pit for dinner.

food.name: Rfiss and tamina
food.desc: Sweets built from the same pantry: crumbled bread or roasted semolina worked with dates, butter and honey into a dense, spiced dish for guests.

places.name: Timimoun central souk
places.note: Sweet stalls sell date paste, honey and roasted semolina, plus ready-made rfiss.

places.name: Guesthouses in the ksour
places.note: Made at home for weddings and for visitors; served with mint tea.

places.name: Hotel Gourara
places.note: Date-based sweets and pastries appear on the dessert table and at breakfast.

food.name: Mint tea
food.desc: Strong green tea boiled with sugar and fresh mint, poured from height into small glasses and served in rounds; Timimoun is dry, so tea is the social drink.

places.name: Hotel Gourara terrace
places.note: Tea on the terrace at sunset with the palmeraie and salt flat below.

places.name: Town centre cafes, Rue Principale
places.note: Men's cafes near the souk pour tea and strong coffee all day; cheap and welcoming.

places.name: Desert camps, Grand Erg Occidental
places.note: Guides brew tea over the fire as the standard end to a desert evening.

food.name: Lben and date juice
food.desc: Lben is tangy churned buttermilk drunk cold with couscous; date juice and date milkshakes are the sweet oasis alternative, both alcohol free.

places.name: Timimoun central souk
places.note: Dairy sellers bottle fresh lben each morning; date drinks sold beside them.

places.name: Hotel Gourara restaurant
places.note: Lben and fresh juices come with the set lunch and dinner menus.

places.name: Hotel de l'Oasis Rouge
places.note: Cafe side of the old hotel serves cold buttermilk and date-based drinks.

landmarks: Old Ksar of Timimoun
The red-ochre old town's crenellated mud-brick walls, studded gates and shaded passageways embody Sudanese-Saharan architecture, glowing crimson at sunset over the oasis.
Porte du Soudan (Sudan Gate)
Timimoun's emblematic neo-Sudanese gateway of spiked ochre towers once marked the caravan road toward sub-Saharan Africa and remains the town's favourite photo stop.
Hôtel de l'Oasis Rouge
A 1917 colonial hotel built in grand Sudanese style, whose sculpted red facades hosted writers and film crews drawn to the 'red oasis'.
Palmeraie of Timimoun
A vast palm grove of gardens and irrigation channels stretches below the town, where farmers tend dates, vegetables and fruit beneath rustling green canopies.
Grande Sebkha Viewpoint
From the escarpment's edge, gaze across the immense salt-lake depression toward distant dunes, an unforgettable panorama that defines the Gourara region's stark beauty.
Foggara Irrigation Galleries
Ingenious underground channels, some centuries old, still carry water from distant aquifers to the palm gardens, a UNESCO-recognised marvel of Saharan hydraulic engineering.
Ksar Ouled Saïd
A beautifully preserved fortified village near Timimoun whose earthen mosque, granaries and labyrinthine alleys showcase traditional Gourara oasis life.
Grand Erg Occidental Dunes at Tinerkouk
Day trips north reach towering golden dunes of the Great Western Erg, where camel rides and sunset climbs deliver the quintessential Sahara experience.
Old Mosque of Timimoun
The town's venerable mud-brick mosque, with its tapering Sudanese-style minaret, anchors the ksar's spiritual life and the Sufi traditions of the Gourara.
Timimoun Market
The lively central souk trades dates, woven baskets, silver jewellery and desert produce, drawing Zenete Berber, Arab and Haratin communities from surrounding oases.

train.note: There is no railway in the Algerian Sahara - SNTF (https://www.sntf.dz/) does not reach anywhere near Timimoun. Access is by long desert road or by the small airport, which has flights from Algiers a few times a week.

bus.note: No international coaches - the southern borders with Mali and Niger are closed to travellers. SNTV coaches connect Timimoun with Adrar in about 3 hours and Algiers in around 15, running only once or twice a day. Buy at the terminal in cash and check current security advice for the Saharan routes.

ferry.note: Timimoun is an oasis town in the Grand Erg Occidental with no water beyond the palm-grove irrigation channels, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Charouine
half.blurb: Charouine is a Saharan oasis village in the Gourara region with palm groves and traditional earthen ksar architecture.

full.name: Adrar
full.blurb: Adrar is a regional capital south of Timimoun with its own mudbrick ksour, an ancient irrigation system and desert markets.
